To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Relatively Quantified Formulas with a basis of predicates are polynomially learnable from equivalence queries if and only if every predicate is polynomially learnable.
Relatively Quantified Formulas are either learnable with equivalence or membership queries, or not predictable with membership queries.
Relatively Quantified Formulas are either polynomially predictable, or not polynomial-time learnable, depending on the basis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: what makes a quantified formula learnable? We provide a simple answer to this question in terms of the basis.
the following questions: Given a set of predicates P and an integer n, what are the learnability and predictability properties of the class of formulas over n variables that use predicates in P?
the following question: given a set of predicates (a basis), how complex are the formulas that can be built using the predicates in this basis?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the learnability of Relatively-Quantified-Formulas (RQFs) is determined by the basis.
the class of RQGF is learnable with equivalence query, and is not learnable with membership query.
the learnability of the Relatively Quantified Formulas depends on the basis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, the learning complexity of Relatively Quantifed Generalized Formulas is determined by its basis.
, the learnability of a class of formulas is determined by the learnability of the formulas in the basis.
, in the context of learnability of quantified formulas, the class of Relatively Quantifed Generalized Formulas is the most general class that has been studied so far.
The main takeaway from our work is that

learning complexity is highly sensitive to quantifier structure and that the complexity of a class of quantified formulas can be drastically different even when the underlying predicates are identical.
learning relatively quantified formulas is in general as hard as learning DNFs.
the learnability of quantified formulas can depend on the underlying basis, and that the basis can have a significant impact on the learning complexity.
